DONALD DELUE (1897-1988)
Studies for Swimming Medal (a group of eleven) 
each unsigned and one annotated
first through tenth charcoal and graphite on paper and eleventh charcoal, graphite and pen on paper
sheet sizes to 14 x 17 in.

Provenance

The Kalos Agathos Foundation, directly commissioned from the above.

Through his foundation, Bruce Hopping commissioned leading sculptors to create awards and monuments that celebrate the human form in motion, particularly in aquatics and Olympic sports. The works in the present lot were created by Donald De Lue for a 1965 CIF swimming medallion commission. DeLue produced a number of ideas for Hopping to select from over the course of 3-4 weeks completing 24-25 drawings which conveyed his thoughts on swimming: 

'In my drawings I think of Man when swimming as enjoying a closer relationship with all of nature than he does at any other time. There is the sea with all its vastness, power and majesty, the sun in all its splendor, as what would the beach and swimming be without the sun and the air and sky. Therefore man is at one with all of this wonderful relationship. This gives him a sense of great wellbeing.' — Letter from Donald DeLue to Bruce Hopping, July 28, 1966 

The typed letter on Donald DeLue's letterhead accompanies the lot.

description_block:
DONAL HORD (1902-1966)
The Swimmer 
bronze with brown patina
38 in. high, on a 3 3/4 in. high base
Modeled and cast circa 1965.

Provenance
The artist.
The Kalos Agathos Foundation, commissioned from the above.

The Kalos Agathos Foundation was officially created in 1968, its predecessor organization, the New Jersey Committee began in 1953 when, after the death of his father, Founding Director Bruce Hopping used his inheritance to create a foundation that would promote swimming as an ideal form of exercise. For the next 15 years, Director Hopping worked through the New Jersey Committee, sponsoring aquatic sport forums and competitions, as well as commissioning works of art to be given as the foremost prestigious awards and honors in the realms of amateur competitive swimming and diving. 

In 1961, Director Hopping relocated from Maplewood, New Jersey to Laguna Beach, California. Already by that time, Laguna Beach was well-established as an international travel destination devoted to the arts and various ocean sports like surfing, bodyboarding, and rowing. Throughout the 1960s, the activities of the New Jersey Committee broadened in scope to include these other forms of aquatic sports, surfing foremost among them, while also actively endorsing projects to support the visual and performing arts and ocean ecology. Hopping was also a pioneer in youth sports diplomacy - sponsoring exchanges with nearly 50 countries and impacting thousands of young people. The foundation was also supporting visual, performing, and literary arts from the 1960s onward, by conceiving of and administering cultural exchanges and endowing grants and awards.

Through his foundation, Bruce Hopping commissioned leading sculptors to create awards and monuments that celebrate the human form in motion, particularly in aquatics and Olympic sports. The foundation's most visible presence in Hawaiʻi is the Toots Minvielle Memorial Sculpture honoring A.E. "Toots" Minvielle, the patriarch of Hawaiian outrigger canoe racing donated to the state of Hawaiʻi by the foundation.

Hopping commissioned two works by Donal Hord. The first, and the present lot became a signature symbol of the organization, in one period document, it is described as:

The Kalos Agathos sculpture, commissioned by the foundation to emulate the bronze statues erected (884-394 B.C.) by the Greeks to honor the revered athletes of sacred Olympia, symbolizes the Foundation philosophy which relates directly to the ancient Greek ideal of youth education... striving for Kalos Agathos: Physical Distinction – Nobility of Mind.

The figure, modeled after athlete Robbie Handler (a swimmer and gymnast) exhibits exceptional accuracy in a classical form. This bronze served as the model for another Hopping commission, the Swedish Swimming Federation Award. The award, another sculpture by Hord, features Handler in a different pose on a similar base and was presented in 1965 to the Swedish Swimming Federation.

In June of 1863 Albert Bierstadt accompanied William Byers, publisher of The Rocky Mountain News on a tour of the dramatic high-country scenery in the Chicago Lakes area near Idaho Springs, west of Denver. Rosalie, named after Bierstadt's future wife, in the 20th Century Colorado lawmakers renamed the peak to Mount Evans and today it is known as Mount Blue Sky.

Eanger Irving Couse was born in Saginaw, Michigan and was interested in drawing from an early age. As a young man, Couse visited and sketched the local Ojibwa Indian settlements and was generally fascinated by the Ojibwa peoples' history and folklore. 

Despite a deep desire to pursue a career as an artist, Couse's father was unsupportive, and Couse worked as a house and barn painter in order to make enough money to attend first the Art Institute in Chicago and then the National Academy of Design in New York. Success was almost immediate for the artist and he was winning medals for his work in his first year in New York. 

In 1886, Couse saved enough money to travel to Paris for a year's study at the Académie Julien and the École des Beaux-Arts. His exposure in France to master draftsman and instructor Adolphe Bouguereau had a profound influence on the artist's work. In 1891, Couse returned to the US for a few years and initially spent time with his wife Virginia's family in Oregon where he painted his first Native American subjects: the Klickitat, Yakima and Umatilla peoples. The subsequent decade was spent in France, on the East Coast and again in Oregon. At the suggestion of Joseph Henry Sharp, Ernest Blumenschein and Bert Geer Phillips, whom he had met in Paris, Couse visited Taos for the first time by train in 1902. "Taos was everything Couse had dreamed of. The Taos people and their routines of life at the Pueblo satisfied all of his artistic requirements and desires. He recognized that in the Pueblos of the Southwest he had found the ideal Indian subjects for his paintings." 1 

Between 1904 and 1927, Couse spent summers painting and living in Taos until finally moving permanently to the area in his 60s. Although Couse's work can be romanticized, in his personal life he had close friendships and associations with a number of Taos people who posed for him. Couse's training in anatomy is evident in his frequent use of dramatic side light to accentuate the muscular and skin tone of his Taos Indian subjects. 

In works such as The Chant, the fire's glow lends intimacy to the scene and enhances the overall dramatic effect. The figure squats beside his drum, gently pounding out a methodic rhythm, eyes closed and rapt in prayerful concentration. A fire keeps the interior colors warm, the yellow and orange glow engulfs the composition in a warm blanket of color. Couse succeeds in presenting the viewer with a deceptively simple composition, a lone figure in an interior, but with a balance of wonderful color, drama and romance. The darkness of the interior is offset by the exquisite turquoise blue in the figure's moccasins and hair beads. His arms and face catch the glow of the fire enhancing his strong profile, while the light-colored drum, feathers and chaps give weight to the scene in a balanced triangle. The result is an intimate portrait of a local Pueblo man in a moment of ritual life.

Used for the Santa Fe Railroad Company's 1935 calendar, the present work was actually painted a few years prior to publication, in 1926. Usually Couse's calendar commissions were planned and executed one to two years in advance, but sometimes painting publications were further postponed. 2

While many of Dixon's illustrations are often a result of tall tales of the American West, Mexico's Trouble Maker is rooted in current events. The present work was completed during the height of the Mexican Revolution mere months after Francisco Madero was elected President following the resignation of longtime dictator Porfirio Díaz. Madero would only serve as President for just over a year before being assassinated in a coup d'état. While Madero was generally well received by many Mexicans at the start of his short-lived presidency, some revolutionaries, particularly Emiliano Zapata and his followers, felt Madero was not moving quickly enough on land reform. As a result of the continued unrest, Zapata's guerrilla efforts were often portrayed as banditry to contemporary American audiences. Dixon's action-packed illustration adds a visual narrative to Avirette's primary source account, bringing to life events unfolding across the border.

MAYNARD DIXON (1875-1946)
The End of the Game 
signed and dated 'Maynard Dixon / 1912' (lower left) and inscribed with a passage from The Long Chance (on the reverse)
oil on board
27 3/4 x 19 in.
Painted in 1912.

Provenance
Medicine Man Gallery Inc., Tucson, Arizona. 
Property from a Rancho Mirage Philanthropist, acquired from the above 2001. 

Literature
Peter B. Kyne, "The Long Chance," Sunset Magazine, September 1913, p. 529, illustrated.

'Nobody knows the West better than Dixon, and he never put it into better pictures than the twenty he has made for "The Long Chance."' Sunset Magazine, 1912

In his seminal monograph Maynard Dixon: Artist of the West, Wesley Burnside characterized Dixon's oeuvre as a dichotomy of styles: "Western Genre and American landscape tradition." Western genre emphasized man's struggle for survival on the frontier with insights into the life of cowboys and range border disputes. These episodic events then often became melodramatic and spectacular, particularly as described by many authors and illustrators of popular magazines of the day. 1 The present lot is one such rousing and epic illustration in the Western genre that Maynard Dixon created for Peter Kyne's 'The Long Chance.'

Published across twenty installments beginning with the 1912 Christmas Edition of Sunset Magazine, 'The Long Chance' follows Bob McGraw, a determined prospector and entrepreneur, as he pursues fortune in the California desert. Ahead of the first installment the magazine announced the forthcoming serialization in its November 1912 issue teasing that, "Peter B. Kyne, prince of short-story tellers, has written a Western novel, and Maynard Dixon -Remington's successor- Has illustrated it." 2. The series opens with Last Lap (sold at Bonhams in 2023), a scene that foreshadows Bob's trials and quixotic wanderings in the desert. The story then reverts to an earlier point in Bob's journey with Farewell (now in the collection of the Brigham Young Museum of Art) where he bids goodbye to the novel's female protagonist, Donna Corblay. Left in the gritty mining town of San Pasqual, Donna's life soon becomes intertwined with local gambler and saloon owner Harley P. Hennage. Although Hennage is first introduced as a morally ambiguous character, in Bob's absence he becomes a father figure to Donna. End of the Game comes from the penultimate chapter when Hennage confronts Borax O'Rourke in an effort to protect Donna. Painted in grisaille, the work captures Hennage with an arm outstretched in a moment of fleeting victory as a crowd gathers in the distance. Before succumbing to his own fatal wounds, Hennage remains conscious long enough to see Bob and Donna reunited, providing a poignant resolution to his sacrifice as he makes a 'dignified exit from the story.' 

Dixon's career as an illustrator started in 1895 when he was hired by the San Francisco Morning Call to provide views of Western life for their Sunday edition. The pressures of meeting these weekly deadlines honed Dixon's skills as a draftsman and he quickly learned to draw with speed without sacrificing accuracy. After the 1906 earthquake destroyed Dixon's studio he briefly moved to New York where he found further success with commissions for periodicals like Harper's Weekly and Scribner's Magazine. Dixon would remain in New York until 1912 when the commission for 'The Long Chance' finally brought him back West. Dixon's post New York period marks the beginning of his transition from serialized Western genre scenes that established his reputation toward the sweeping American landscapes for which he would become best remembered.

description_block:
EDGAR PAYNE (1883-1947)
Riders on the Mesa (Indian Riders) 
signed 'EDGAR PAYNE' (lower left)
oil on canvas
25 1/4 x 30 in.

Provenance
DeVille Galleries, Los Angeles.
Property from an Important Southern California Collection, acquired from the above.

Literature
E. Cohen, "California Dreaming," Interior Design, January 1997, vol. 68, no. 1, p. 123, illustrated.

One of California's most important Impressionist painters, Edgar Payne's legacy remains his lifelong dedication to travel and exploration, erudition in art theory, and mastery of technique. Born and raised in the Midwest, Payne traversed the world from Europe to Southern California in search of the sublime in nature, expressed through landscape painting. Unlike the earlier generation of California painters inspired by the Hudson River School who 'envisioned the world in static scenes, Payne recorded a serially changing landscape that captured fleeting moments in nature — light, color, clouds — through rhythm, movement, dynamic compositions and expressive brushwork.'1

Payne was dedicated to his craft for nearly four decades, producing significant bodies of work in the Swiss and French Alps, on the Brittany Coast, on the Venetian lagoon, in Southern California (particularly Laguna Beach and the Eastern Sierras) and the American Southwest. 

Of all of his subjects that 'beckoned him as a muse, the American Southwest was perhaps the most compelling.' 2 Payne first encountered the region in 1909 on his first trip to California, passing through Arizona and New Mexico aboard the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway. By 1915, Payne was working between Chicago and California for private and commercial clients. Spurred on by expanded railway service in the West and Southwest — particularly the development of a new Santa Fe Railway passenger train — Payne ventured to Canyon de Chelly on the Navajo Reservation for a commissioned project. The canyon's monolithic structure and its monumental scale to the surrounding desert inspired him for the rest of his life. 

Riders on the Mesa (Indian Riders) is a superlative example of Payne's work in the Southwest. The work captures the region's characteristic 'big sky' occupying two-thirds of the composition. In the present work, figures serve as compositional devices to heighten the scale and grandeur of the cloudscape. Along with Canyon de Chelly, desert scenes on the Navajo Reservation are well-represented in Payne's body of work. He revisited this particular vantage point over several works including Untitled [Clouds and Riders], n.d., Two Indians in Southwest Landscape, after 1929, and Navajo Country, 1942. What distinguishes the present work, however, is Payne's treatment of light. Through contrasting color values, Payne conveys the ephemeral and dramatic nature of atmospheric conditions in the Southwest. True to the tenets of Impressionism espoused by Claude Monet, the atmosphere is the true subject, and the technique is in service of it. 

The present work held pride of place with the family of the current owners for decades. Styled in a timeless interior by the inimitable Barbara Barry, the work served as one of two focal points within seating groups in their formal living room. The expansive vista of Riders on the Mesa (Indian Riders) was placed as a visual counterweight to the bustling Manhattan view of John Grabach's At the Plaza (see American Art, Bonhams New York, November 3, 2026, Lot 73). Held together, the works represented visual bookends of their collection from coast to coast.
